lead: Oklahoma City sits in the heart of Tornado Alley, and its homes take hail, wind and tornadoes almost every spring. Storm leaks and freeze damage drive most of its water damage.
risk: hail and tornado damage, roof leaks and frozen pipes
why: Spring storms in central Oklahoma are some of the strongest anywhere. Large hail cracks shingles and breaks skylights, and straight-line winds peel back roofs. On May 3, 1999, a violent tornado tore through south Oklahoma City and Moore, and another struck Moore in May 2013. Even when a tornado misses, a damaged roof lets rain pour into attics, ceilings and walls in the storms that follow.

Most Oklahoma City homes sit on slabs, with few basements. That keeps flood damage lower, but water from roof leaks and burst pipes spreads across floors fast. In February 2021, a deep freeze split pipes in attics and outside walls across the city. Oklahoma City is also huge in area, so many homes are on rural lots with well pumps and long supply lines.
image_alt: Aerial view of a long tornado track across a town
image_caption: Tornadoes have cut long paths through Oklahoma City and its suburbs.
problems: Attic and outside-wall pipes in hard freezes
tips: Get the roof checked after any hail, even with no leak yet.
Know your wind and hail deductible before storm season.
Insulate attic pipes and open cabinet doors on freeze nights.
Have a safe room or plan for tornado warnings.
areas: Calls come from Bricktown, Midtown, Mesta Park, Heritage Hills, Paseo, Crown Heights, Capitol Hill and Deep Deuce, plus Edmond, Moore, Norman and Yukon.

faq.q: How fast should I tarp my Oklahoma City roof after hail?
faq.a: As soon as it is safe. Insurers expect you to prevent more damage, and another storm can come within days. Take photos first, then tarp any holes or missing shingles. DryFlare can dry the attic, insulation and ceilings so mold does not start.
